Most of the country is currently in the off-season, with Season B crops including beans, sorghum, and maize fully harvested. Yield prospects are at or slightly below average, reflecting poor rainfall performance throughout the season linked to the persisting El Niño episode. Above-average temperatures have been recorded across the country over the last three dekads, with peaks reaching +7% above the long-term average in Gitega. [https://agricultural-production-hotspots.ec.europa.eu/seasonal_forecast.php?sfreg=africa] Seasonal forecasts from the Copernicus Climate Change Service indicate above-average rainfall in Burundi during the OND rainy season. According to [https://reliefweb.int/report/burundi/wfp-burundi-country-brief-august-2026] WFP, the 2026 Season B harvest brought continued seasonal relief, improving food availability compared to June, with 66 percent of key informants reporting increased stocks. However, supplies remain below July 2025 levels due to drought in the north and flooding in the west, with most staple food prices still above their five-year average reflecting structural market pressures.

Vegetation conditions in the north/eastern parts of Kenya deteriorated further in August, reflecting a rapid deterioration of pastoral vegetation in the ASALs. This is due to cumulative effects of below-average rainfall since late May and throughout June and July as well as above average temperatures. In the unimodal cropping zones, below-average rainfall slowed crop development and reduced soil moisture availability during critical crop growth stages causing clearly below average crop production expectations both in Western Kenya and in the Rift Valley counties, Kenya's main bread basket. Looking ahead, forecasts of a strong El Niño for the upcoming short rains season point to above average rainfall. It is important however to bear in mind that high intensity rainfall will not be immediately beneficial to drought affected crop areas and that there is a high risk of adverse impacts including increased risk of flooding. These conditions could further affect agricultural production, disrupt livelihoods, and complicate recovery efforts in areas already impacted by the current dry spell.

In Madagascar, apart from areas where secondary rice planting is underway, there are no cereals growing now and in the central and northern areas, the next rice season is expected to start in November with the arrival of the rainy season. In the Grand South (Anosy, Androy and Atsimo Andrefana), the next cereals season should start in October and drier than average conditions are expected in the western half of the country (including Atsimo Andrefana) according to the C3S multimodel seasonal forecast.

Most of the country is currently in the off-season as season B crops including beans, sorghum, and maize have been fully harvested. Yield prospects are below average due to poor rainfall performance throughout the season, linked to the persisting El Niño episode. Average temperature has been recorded above average throughout the country during the last three dekads, with peaks of +11% against the long-term average in Nyagatare. According to [https://reliefweb.int/report/rwanda/wfp-rwanda-country-brief-august-2026] WFP, recent harvests have nonetheless improved the availability of staple foods, contributing to stable food basket costs and price reductions, particularly in more productive regions. Looking ahead, Rwanda is forecast to receive above-average rainfall during the OND rainy season, as pointed by the [https://agricultural-production-hotspots.ec.europa.eu/seasonal_forecast.php?sfreg=africa] seasonal forecasts from the Copernicus Climate Change Service.
Not a hotspot country according to the latest ASAP analysis.

The Msimu crop harvest (sorghum, rice and maize) has been completed in unimodal areas, while the Masika harvest (sorghum, millet and maize) is still underway in bimodal areas. Precipitation has been average throughout the country in the last 30 days. Below average biomass conditions are present in Morogoro and Pwani, where 27% and 36% of the active crop area is seen in poor vegetation status. The current El Niño episode, hitting with dry conditions in particular the north of the country, is expected to [https://agricultural-production-hotspots.ec.europa.eu/seasonal_forecast.php?sfreg=africa] shift to wet conditions in October. In this context, Tanzania's Deputy Minister for Agriculture urged citizens on August 26 to [https://www.therespondents.co.tz/2026/08/silinde-urges-tanzanians-to-store-food.html] preserve harvested food stocks, warning that the anticipated above-average rainfall could disrupt agricultural production and heighten food insecurity risks in the coming season. According to [https://reliefweb.int/report/united-republic-tanzania/wfp-tanzania-country-brief-august-2026] WFP, while agriculture remains central to livelihoods and national growth, climate shocks, rising fuel and input costs continue to pose risks to food systems and vulnerable households, reinforcing the importance of climate-smart agriculture and shock-responsive social protection.

Poor and inconsistent rainfall from June to August together with high temperatures prevailed in the unimodal areas of Karamoja pointing to low harvest expectations. Similar conditions but in a more patchy patter are also visible in the eastern and central parts of the country and might locally hamper planting of second season crops in the bimodal areas. According to [https://fews.net/east-africa/uganda" target="_blank] FEWSNET the increased refugee numbers in Karamoja, together with the poor harvest and high food prices contributes to rapidly increasing humanitarian needs. Patches of worsening vegetation conditions shown by satellite imagery in the east and central parts of the country also point towards decreasing rangeland availability for livestock.
Not a hotspot country according to the latest ASAP analysis.
